w: Completed around 100 BC to carry the Via Postumia across the Adige, this is Verona's oldest bridge and once had a Roman twin alongside it. Retreating German troops dynamited four of its arches in 1945; in 1957 it was rebuilt using the original Roman materials fished back out of the river.
s: Verona's oldest bridge, rebuilt from its own stones
_facts: Completed 100 BC, carried the Via Postumia
Oldest bridge in Verona
Four arches destroyed by German troops in WWII
Rebuilt 1957 with original materials

w: Once the forum of Roman Verona, this square has been doing business in one form or another for two thousand years - market stalls, awnings and cafe tables now cover the ground where togas and senators once walked. The name means 'square of herbs,' a nod to centuries as the city's produce market.
s: The Roman forum that never stopped trading
_facts: Was the town's Roman forum
Name translates to 'Market's square'
Still functions as a market square today

w: Housed inside a genuine medieval castle, this museum owes its striking modern feel to architect Carlo Scarpa, who spent fourteen years reworking every doorway, staircase and display case by hand. His approach, blending old stone with new intervention, became a template for how museums renovate historic buildings.
s: A medieval castle rebuilt by a modernist master
_facts: Museum inside the medieval Castelvecchio
Restored by architect Carlo Scarpa, 1959-1973
Scarpa's approach balanced old and new, now a common renovation model

w: The name Bra comes from a dialect word simply meaning 'wide,' and this became Verona's largest square by accretion - a 16th-century palazzo, an Austrian-built Gran Guardia, and the Liston promenade paved in 1770 for the city's rising bourgeoisie. Palazzo Barbieri, once Austrian barracks, is now the town hall.
s: Verona's grand square, named for being 'wide'
_facts: Name derives from Lombardic 'breit', meaning wide
Largest public square in Verona
Liston promenade first paved 1770
Palazzo Barbieri became Verona's municipal headquarters after unification

w: Built to defend Castelvecchio and give the ruling Scaliger family an escape route across the Adige, this fortified bridge held the record for the world's widest arch span at the time of its construction, at 48.70 metres. Crenellated like the castle it serves, it still carries traffic across the river today.
s: A fortified bridge with the world's longest span
_facts: Also called Ponte Scaligero, a fortified bridge over the Adige
Held the world's largest arch span at construction, 48.70 metres

w: Verona's largest and most solemn church rose through the Gothic era with backing from the ruling Scaliger family, the Dominican order and the wealthy Castelbarco clan - visible in its wide transept and four-chapel apse. Its facade was never finished, though a grand Gothic doorway survives to prove what might have been.
s: Verona's biggest church, with an unfinished face
_facts: Largest, most solemn church in Verona
Built with backing from the Scaliger rule, Dominican clergy, Castelbarco family
Facade left unfinished except for a Gothic mullioned doorway

w: Five Gothic funerary monuments crowd this small walled courtyard, each built for a member of the Scaliger family who ruled Verona from the 13th to the late 14th century. Sarcophagi topped with armoured equestrian statues rise above iron grilles - historian Georges Duby called them outstanding Gothic art.
s: Gothic tombs for the family that once ruled Verona
_facts: Five Gothic funerary monuments for the Scaliger family
Family ruled Verona 13th to late 14th century
Sarcophagi topped with mounted, armoured statues
Called outstanding Gothic art by historian Georges Duby

w: Verona's Roman theatre sits quietly on the Adige's east bank, often confused with - and overshadowed by - the city's famous Roman amphitheatre across town. Reached in Roman times via the Ponte Pietra, it once anchored the same riverside district as the stone bridge that still stands beside it.
s: The Roman theatre overshadowed by the arena
_facts: Ancient Roman theatre on the east bank of the Adige
Distinct from the Verona Arena amphitheatre
Historically accessed via the Ponte Pietra

w: Expanded to three storeys in 1469 by nobleman Marcantonio Maffei and finished nearly two centuries later, this Baroque palace stands on ancient remains of Verona's Roman Capitoline Hill. Six marble statues of the gods line its roof, while inside, a bizarre spiral stone staircase corkscrews from cellar to roof.
s: A Baroque palace hiding a spiral staircase
_facts: Expanded to three floors from 1469 by Marcantonio Maffei
Construction finished 1668
Built above remains of the Roman Capitoline Hill
Roof balustrade has six statues of Hercules, Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, Apollo, Minerva
Interior has a helicoidal stone staircase

w: Built by the wealthy Gavia family to celebrate themselves rather than the state, this rare privately funded Roman arch became a must-study monument for Renaissance architects like Palladio and Sanmicheli. French engineers blew it up in 1805; old surveys let it be reassembled stone by stone in 1932, near Castelvecchio.
s: A private family's Roman arch, rebuilt from scratch
_facts: Rare privately funded Roman monumental arch, built for the gens Gavia
Studied by Renaissance architects including Palladio and Sanmicheli
Demolished by French military engineers in 1805
Reassembled by anastylosis in 1932 near Castelvecchio

w: This 1st-century Roman gate once carried the Via Postumia into Verona and was decorated richly enough to impress every traveler passing through. Originally dedicated to Jupiter as the Porta Iovia, it later took its current name from the toll collectors, or bursarii, who worked its arches in the Middle Ages.
s: A richly carved Roman gate on the old main road
_facts: Dates to the 1st century AD, over an earlier 1st-century BC gate
Original Roman name Porta Iovia, near a temple to Jupiter
Current name from medieval toll collectors, bursarii
Via Postumia passed through as the decumanus maximus

w: Built during the Roman Republic and refitted under the empire, this gate once guarded the road toward Bologna and Aquileia through a pair of towers on a double facade. Its current name has nothing to do with its own decoration - it comes from a nearby Roman tomb carved with two lions, since moved elsewhere in the city.
s: A gate named for lions on a tomb, not itself
_facts: Roman Republic-era gate, restructured in imperial times
Connected to the road to Bologna and Aquileia
Name comes from a nearby Roman tomb decorated with two lions

w: Michele Sanmicheli designed this gate in the mid-16th century to punch through Verona's outer walls, giving it robust Doric columns that read as strength rather than decoration. It replaced a medieval portal used for a horse race called the Palio - the origin of the name that survived the gate's total rebuild.
s: A Renaissance gate named for a medieval race
_facts: Designed by Michele Sanmicheli, built 1550-1561
Part of the former outer medieval walls
Named after a Palio horse race held at the earlier medieval portal

w: Started in 1172 and struck by lightning in 1403, this 84-metre tower took sixteen years to repair and grew taller in the process - newer marble sections are still visible against the older stone. Two bells hang inside: the Marangona, which warned of fires, and the larger Rengo, rung to call citizens to arms.
s: An 84-metre tower rung by two named bells
_facts: Construction began 1172, tower is 84m tall
Struck by lightning in 1403, repairs from 1448 for 16 years
Houses the Marangona bell (fires, work hours) and the larger Rengo bell (calls to arms/council)
Rengo used during the 1797 Veronese Easter revolt

w: Conceived in the 1930s by architect Angelo Invernizzi, this house near Verona does something no ordinary villa does: it rotates, tracking the sun across the sky like the flower it's named for - il girasole, the sunflower. A mechanical marvel disguised as a home, it remains one of the stranger buildings in the region.
s: The 1930s house that rotates to follow the sun
_facts: Built in the 1930s in Marcellise, near Verona
Designed by architect Angelo Invernizzi
The house physically rotates to follow the sun
